lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mark Kazuyoshi Seki Omagari | Lesson 21 -- Once Upon a Time Online
lesson.grammar_point: narrative tenses (past continuous and past perfect continuous in contrast)

listenings.text: Hi Mark. Last class you used the past perfect to say which thing happened first, and today we put that tense back into the middle of a whole story. When you retell an episode online, you almost never use one tense. You use three or four at the same time, and each one has a different job. The past simple carries the chain of events, so first this happened, then that happened. The past continuous paints the background, so it tells us what was already going on when the main event arrived. The past perfect goes one step further back, to something that had happened before the story even started. And the past perfect continuous, which is the new one today, tells us how long something had been going on up to that moment. Listen for the difference between she was waiting and she had been waiting. The first one is background. The second one gives you the duration, and it usually explains why the character reacted the way she did. Try this before class. Take the last episode you watched, and describe the first two minutes using at least three different past tenses. See you on Wednesday, Mark.

So I finally watched the episode everybody was posting about, and I want to explain why the ending works. It opens quietly. Two characters were walking through an empty station, talking about nothing important, and the camera was following them from behind. Nothing had happened yet, and that is exactly the point, because the show had been building this moment for six episodes. Then the lights went out. The protagonist stopped, turned around, and realized that the person she had been travelling with for the whole season was not there anymore. The backstory lands in one line: she had been looking for her brother since the first episode, and the show had never told us why. And then the credits roll. That is the cliffhanger, and it is a cruel one, because the subplot about the letters suddenly makes sense and the main plot suddenly does not. I watched it twice. The second time I noticed that the red herring had been sitting in the background of every single scene, and I had walked straight past it.

extra_audio.text: First, you set the scene with the past continuous, so you say what was already going on when the story starts. Then you drop in the first event with the past simple, and that event usually interrupts the background. After that, if you need to explain something that happened even earlier, you step back with the past perfect. Next, if the point is how long that earlier thing had been going on, you use the past perfect continuous instead. Finally, you return to the past simple and carry the chain of events to the end of the story.
